content: The World Health Organization (WHO) in 2014 aimed to develop consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. This effort sought to integrate existing WHO guidance with new material to address identified gaps. The guidelines were designed to address common elements across all key populations while also highlighting unique issues specific to individual groups. As part of this process, the WHO commissioned the Global Forum on MSM and HIV (MSMGF) to conduct a qualitative study exploring the values and preferences of men who have sex with men (MSM) globally, particularly regarding the use of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP). MSM are disproportionately affected by HIV, with a 19-fold higher likelihood of infection compared to the general population in lowand middle-income countries. HIV prevalence among MSM is consistently higher than in the general population across nearly all countries with reliable surveillance data. For instance, studies from as early as 2002 revealed that HIV infection rates among MSM in Latin America were significantly higher than in the general population, with rates seven times higher in Honduras, 10 times higher in Guatemala and Panama, 22 times higher in El Salvador, and 38 times higher in Nicaragua. This pattern is also observed in Africa, Asia, Eastern Europe, and the Caribbean. Biomedical interventions, such as PrEP and early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), have demonstrated significant potential in preventing HIV transmission among MSM and serodiscordant heterosexual couples. Observational and ecological studies have further supported the association between HIV treatment and reductions in new infections. However, structural, interpersonal, and individual factors influence access to and uptake of these interventions. MSM globally face widespread human rights abuses, discrimination, and criminalization, with 76 countries imposing criminal penalties for consensual same-sex acts as of May 2010. Such criminalization and violence exacerbate social dislocation, fuel transnational migration, and heighten the risk of HIV transmission, while also deterring those most in need from accessing prevention, care, treatment, and support services. Understanding the values and preferences of MSM regarding ART as prevention is critical, particularly within the contexts in which they live. The MSMGF project team, formed in January 2014, included experts who developed protocols for secondary data analyses and qualitative analyses of ART-related narratives. The WHO reviewed and approved these protocols, after which data collection and analysis commenced. The 2012 Global Men’s Health and Rights (GMHR) study included a global online survey assessing the availability of and access to STI and HIV testing and prevention services among MSM across eight regions. A total of 4,005 respondents participated, with 17% aged 24 years or younger and 81% having post-secondary education. Participants were broadly representative of various regions, including Western and Northern Europe, North America, Asia, Eastern Europe, Central Asia, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, the Middle East, and the Caribbean. Half of the respondents reported middle to high income, while 18% had low or no income. The study identified predictors of HIV service utilization. Higher community engagement and connection to the community positively influenced the use of HIV prevention services, such as condoms and condom-compatible lubricants, as well as HIV testing. Comfort with healthcare providers was also associated with increased utilization of HIV testing and treatment. Conversely, higher perceptions of homophobia negatively impacted the use of condoms and lubricants. Past experiences of provider stigma were linked to higher utilization of HIV treatment, substance abuse treatment, and in-person behavioral interventions, but not with the use of HIV education materials. Regarding PrEP, the majority of respondents expressed comfort with the concept, though 26% were somewhat or very uncomfortable with using HIV medications to prevent infection. Notably, 52% of participants had low knowledge of PrEP, with many unaware of its existence or purpose. Despite this, 56% reported being likely to use PrEP if approved, with 48% willing to adhere to a daily pill regimen. However, only 19% were likely to use it if associated with uncomfortable side effects. Participants recommended that PrEP be made available in healthcare provider offices, public health clinics, HIV clinics, STI clinics, and non-governmental organizations. Focus group discussions conducted in 2012 with MSM in South Africa, Kenya, and Nigeria revealed structural barriers to accessing HIV services, including criminalization of homosexuality, stigma, discrimination, homophobia in healthcare systems, and poverty. These barriers created environments where blackmail, extortion, discrimination, and violence against MSM persisted. MSM often concealed their sexual behavior from healthcare providers, employers, landlords, teachers, and family to protect themselves and maintain livelihoods. This concealment was associated with misdiagnosis, delayed diagnosis, and delayed treatment. In-depth individual interviews conducted in 2014 with MSM and HIV service providers from diverse countries further explored these issues. Questions focused on experiences with HIV testing, values and preferences regarding ART for prevention, and challenges related to discrimination, violence, and legal issues. The findings highlighted the need to address structural and interpersonal barriers to improve access to and uptake of HIV prevention and treatment services among MSM.
